June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA  
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255 
P.O. Box 8016 
Baltimore, MD 21244-8016 
 
 
Reference: RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory 
Testing (Section III.E of CMS-0062-P) 
 
Re: Comment on RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to 
Laboratory Testing 
 
 
Dear Dr. Oz and Members of the CMS Staff,  
 
On behalf of ICAN, International Cancer Advocacy Network, a 
national cancer patient advocacy organization representing 
patients and families affected by cancer, we appreciate the 
opportunity to provide comments regarding the impact of prior 
authorization requirements on access to laboratory testing.  We 
respectfully request that CMS take prompt, effective action to 
protect our patients, and all patients, from delays and denials for 
laboratory testing caused by prior authorization requirements. 
 
It is important to know a little of ICANâ€™s history to understand 
our perspective on this issue, and how dependent the patients we 
serve are on fast and accurate laboratory testing. ICAN is a 
501(c)(3) non-profit charitable organization (EIN 86-0818253) 
founded in 1996 with a singular mission: to help Stage IV cancer 
patients extend life with the highest achievable quality of life.  
 
Over the past 30 years, ICAN has assisted more than 21,000 late-
stage cancer patients across all 50 states and 93 countriesâ€”
entirely at no cost to patients and families. Our small staff and 
nearly 100 volunteers provide a broad spectrum of services, 
including connecting patients to second opinions and appropriate 
clinical trials, helping patients understand molecular profiling, 
anatomic pathology reports, and molecular diagnoses (both 
germline and somatic).  We connect patients to opportunities for 
compassionate use. 
 
ICAN re Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255, Prior Authorization for Laboratory Testing, page 2 of 3 
 
ICAN also manages the Biomarker Collaborativeâ€”an international consortium of patient groups 
dealing with biomarker-driven diseasesâ€”which emphasizes comprehensive biomarker testing, 
improved screening, and patient engagement. We additionally manage four rare cancer patient 
groups: the Exon 20 Group, MET Crusaders, NRG1 Energizers, and PD-L1 Amplifieds, each 
providing specialized services to patients fighting these specific conditions. 
 
The patients ICAN serves are among the most vulnerable in oncology: individuals with late-stage, 
advanced, or metastatic cancers who have often exhausted standard-of-care options. Many of the 
cancer subtypes we focus onâ€”including those driven by specific biomarkers such as Exon 20 
insertions, MET alterations, NRG1 fusions, and PD-L1 amplificationsâ€”are rare or ultra-rare. For 
many of these patients, time is measured not in years but in months. 
 
Fast, accurate biomarker testing is the key to their treatment. 
 
Our patients depend on timely, accurate biomarker testing to guide treatment decisions. For many 
cancer patients, biomarker testing is not an optional diagnostic procedureâ€”it is the foundation of 
precision medicine and determines whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies, 
immunotherapies, or clinical trials. Delays in obtaining biomarker test results can directly delay the 
initiation of the most effective treatment for a patient's specific cancer. 
 
We commend CMS for seeking stakeholder input regarding how prior authorization requirements 
affect access to laboratory testing, administrative burden, and patient care. We strongly believe that 
prior authorization requirements for biomarker testing create unnecessary barriers that can adversely 
affect patient outcomes. 
 
Cancer treatment decisions increasingly rely on comprehensive biomarker testing. Clinical 
guidelines now recommend biomarker testing for many tumor types, including lung cancer, 
colorectal cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate cancer, and others. These tests identify 
genetic alterations and molecular characteristics that help physicians select therapies that are most 
likely to benefit an individual patient. 
 
Unfortunately, prior authorization requirements frequently delay access to these critical tests. 
Patients often face days or weeks of waiting while laboratories, oncology practices, and health plans 
exchange documentation and respond to requests for additional information. During this period, 
treatment decisions may be postponed, forcing patients and clinicians to wait for authorization 
rather than move forward with evidence-based care. 
 
These delays have significant consequences. Cancer does not pause while administrative processes 
are completed. For patients with aggressive or advanced disease, even short delays can result in 
disease progression, worsening symptoms, increased anxiety, and missed opportunities for optimal 
treatment. Patients and caregivers consistently report that waiting for approval of medically 
necessary testing is among the most stressful aspects of their cancer journey. 
 
Biomarker testing presents unique challenges that make traditional prior authorization approaches 
particularly problematic. In many cases, tissue samples are limited and cannot easily be recollected. 
If testing is delayed or denied after specimen collection, patients may require additional invasive 
procedures to obtain new tissue samples. Furthermore, many biomarker tests are ordered according 
to nationally recognized clinical guidelines and have become standard-of-care components of 
cancer management. 
 
 
 
ICAN re Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255, Prior Authorization for Laboratory Testing, page 3 of 3 
 
Prior authorization requirements also impose substantial administrative burdens on providers and 
laboratories. Oncology practices dedicate significant staff time to obtaining approvals, responding 
to denials, and navigating differing payer requirements. These resources could be better directed 
toward patient care and care coordination. 
 
We know that many patient groups representing cancer patients and those suffering from other 
lethal and chronic diseases, have submitted comments to CMS on this issue.  We wish to associate 
ourselves with these comments and to reiterate what seems to be a basic consensus in urging CMS 
to consider requiring health plans to:  
 
1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected. 
2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing. 
3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available. 
4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing. 
5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative. 
 
Cancer patients deserve timely access to the diagnostic information necessary to guide life-saving 
treatment decisions. Biomarker testing enables precision medicine and helps ensure that patients 
receive the right treatment at the right time. Prior authorization requirements that delay or impede 
access to this testing undermine those goals and place unnecessary burdens on patients, providers, 
and laboratories. 
 
Cancer does not wait, and no health plan should prevent patients from getting fast, accurate, 
biomarker testing, and other tests essential to their care. 
 
If you need any further information, please email me (marcia@askican.org) or call me (602-513-
9217) at your convenience. 
 
Thank you for your consideration. 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,  
Marcia K. Horn  
Marcia K. Horn, JD  
President and CEO  
ICAN, International Cancer Advocacy Network

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** ICAN, International Cancer Advocacy Network; signed by Marcia K. Horn, JD, President and CEO
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** National cancer patient advocacy organization founded in 1996; reports assisting more than 21,000 late-stage cancer patients across all 50 states and 93 countries; manages the Biomarker Collaborative and rare cancer patient groups.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ICAN asks CMS to protect cancer patients from prior authorization delays and denials for laboratory and biomarker testing. The comment emphasizes that timely biomarker testing is central to precision oncology and recommends retroactive authorization, expedited review, limits on timing-based denials, avoidance of repeat specimen collection, and patient protection from surprise costs caused by administrative delays.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL (RFI on prior authorization and access to laboratory testing)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Section III.E of CMS-0062-P; no CFR citations mentioned.
- **Standards referenced:** No FHIR, NCPDP, HL7, or other technical standards referenced.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prior authorization barriers to biomarker testing**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ICAN states that biomarker testing is foundational to precision medicine for patients with advanced, metastatic, rare, and biomarker-driven cancers. PA delays can postpone treatment selection, increase anxiety, and cause clinical harm for patients whose disease may progress quickly.
- **Specific request:** CMS should take prompt action to prevent PA requirements from delaying or denying medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing.

**Topic 2: Retroactive authorization and timing-based denials**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Specimens may already be collected before authorization issues are resolved, and timing-based denials can waste valid specimens and delay care.
- **Specific request:** Require health plans to allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected and prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.

**Topic 3: Avoiding repeat specimen collection**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Cancer tissue samples may be limited and difficult to recollect; unnecessary repeat blood draws or invasive procedures create additional patient burden and risk.
- **Specific request:** Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws or recollection when a valid specimen is available.

**Topic 4: Expedited oncology diagnostic review**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Advanced cancer treatment decisions often depend on rapid test results, and administrative review delays may cause missed treatment opportunities.
- **Specific request:** Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.

**Topic 5: Patient financial protection**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Patients should not bear surprise costs caused by administrative delays outside their control.
- **Specific request:** Protect patients from surprise costs when laboratory testing delays are administrative.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

**Solicitation Responses:**
- **S66-S82:** ICAN responds to the general RFI area addressing laboratory testing and prior authorization. It urges CMS to address PA delays for biomarker testing through retroactive authorization, expedited review, limits on timing-based denials, avoidance of repeat specimens, and patient cost protections.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require health plans to allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
2. Prohibit denials based solely on prior authorization timing.
3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws or repeat tissue collection when a valid specimen is available.
4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
5. Protect patients from surprise costs when testing delays are administrative.
6. Take prompt CMS action to reduce PA-related delays and denials for medically necessary laboratory testing.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** PA delays and denials for biomarker testing; administrative burden on oncology practices and laboratories; patient anxiety and delayed cancer treatment decisions.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Disease progression, worsening symptoms, missed opportunities for targeted therapies, immunotherapies, or clinical trials, additional invasive procedures, and surprise costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Differing payer requirements; documentation exchanges between laboratories, oncology practices, and health plans; limited tissue samples that cannot easily be recollected.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** ICAN states it has assisted more than 21,000 late-stage cancer patients across all 50 states and 93 countries and has nearly 100 volunteers.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No specific studies cited; the comment references nationally recognized clinical guidelines recommending biomarker testing for many tumor types.
- **Examples provided:** Biomarker-driven cancers involving Exon 20 insertions, MET alterations, NRG1 fusions, and PD-L1 amplifications; potential need for additional invasive procedures if testing is delayed or denied after specimen collection.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Cancer patients, caregivers, oncology practices, laboratories, health plans, patient advocacy organizations, and clinicians ordering diagnostic and biomarker tests.
- **Economic implications:** The comment notes potential surprise costs for patients and inefficient provider/laboratory administrative work but does not provide quantified cost estimates.
- **Technical feasibility:** Not addressed from a health IT standards perspective; recommendations focus on payer policy and review-process changes.
- **Patient care impact:** ICAN argues that timely biomarker testing determines access to targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and clinical trials, and that delays can directly harm advanced cancer patients.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned
- **Tone:** Professional, urgent, patient-centered
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Fast, accurate biomarker testing is the key" - Context: ICAN's central patient-care argument.
2. "Cancer does not pause" - Context: Explanation of harm from administrative delay.
3. "Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing" - Context: One of ICAN's requested payer requirements.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - ICAN requests patient protection from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment describes substantial administrative work for oncology practices and laboratories navigating payer requirements.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - ICAN advocates for vulnerable late-stage, rare-cancer, and metastatic cancer patients who may have limited time and few standard treatment options.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The comment's core concern is timely access to laboratory and biomarker testing needed to guide treatment.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - ICAN criticizes traditional PA workflows as poorly suited to biomarker testing where specimens are time-sensitive and sometimes difficult to recollect.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment highlights delays caused by exchanges among laboratories, oncology practices, and health plans.
